content: Only a limited range of services is covered outside the network, typically restricted to emergency care and care provided outside the designated service area. Traditional Health Maintenance Organizations (HMOs) were generally structured as closed network plans. Open network plans, on the other hand, offer some level of coverage when enrollees use non-network providers, though the benefits are usually reduced to encourage the use of in-network providers. Most Preferred Provider Organization (PPO) plans are open-network plans, while those that are not are often referred to as Exclusive Provider Organizations (EPOs). Similarly, Point of Service (POS) plans are also open-network plans. The terms open panel and closed panel are sometimes used to describe the extent to which healthcare providers in a community can participate in a plan. In a closed panel HMO, the network providers are either employees of the HMO (staff model) or members of large group practices contracted by the HMO. In contrast, an open panel plan allows the HMO or PPO to contract with independent practitioners, enabling any provider in the community who meets the plan's credentialing requirements and agrees to the contract terms to participate in the network. Other managed care techniques include disease management, case management, wellness incentives, patient education, utilization management, and utilization review. These strategies can be applied to both network-based benefit programs and those that do not rely on a provider network. When managed care techniques are used without a provider network, the approach is sometimes referred to as managed indemnity. Over time, the operations of many Blue Cross and Blue Shield organizations have become increasingly similar to those of commercial health insurance companies. However, some Blue Cross and Blue Shield plans continue to function as insurers of last resort. Market pressures have led to a convergence in the benefits offered by Blue Cross and Blue Shield plans, commercial insurers, and HMOs. For example, the PPO plans offered by Blue Cross and commercial insurers have become more similar to the POS plans offered by HMOs. It is now common for commercial insurance companies to have HMOs as subsidiaries and vice versa, though the licensing requirements for HMOs and insurance companies typically differ. Historically, the distinctions between traditional indemnity insurance, HMOs, and PPOs were clear, but today, it can be challenging to differentiate between the products offered by these various organizations. The blurring of distinctions between different types of health coverage is also evident in the history of the industry's trade associations. The two primary HMO trade associations, the Group Health Association of America and the American Managed Care and Review Association, merged to form the American Association of Health Plans (AAHP). Similarly, the primary trade association for commercial health insurers, the Health Insurance Association of America (HIAA), has merged with AAHP to create America's Health Insurance Plans (AHIP). One approach to addressing rising insurance premiums, known as consumer-driven healthcare, gained momentum in 2003 when President George W. Bush signed the Medicare Prescription Drug, Improvement, and Modernization Act into law. This legislation introduced tax-deductible Health Savings Accounts (HSAs). An HSA is a tax-advantaged private bank account, with penalties applied only if funds are used for non-medical expenses. To contribute pre-tax funds to an HSA, individuals must be enrolled in a high-deductible insurance plan that meets specific benefit design restrictions. For example, in 2007, qualifying plans required a minimum deductible of $1,050. HSAs allow healthier individuals to pay lower insurance premiums while saving money for future healthcare expenses. HSAs are one type of tax-preferred healthcare spending account, alongside others such as Archer Medical Savings Accounts (MSAs), Flexible Spending Arrangements (FSAs), and Health Reimbursement Accounts (HRAs). HSAs, FSAs, and HRAs are most commonly used as part of employee health benefit packages. Limited Medical Benefit Plans cover routine care but do not provide coverage for catastrophic care, meaning they do not offer the same level of financial security as major medical plans. Annual benefit limits for these plans can be as low as $2,000, with lifetime maximums also being relatively low. Another option gaining popularity is the discount medical card, which provides access to discounts from participating healthcare providers. However, these cards are not insurance policies and may have significant drawbacks for consumers despite offering some value. While the term health insurance is commonly used by the public to refer to coverage for medical expenses, the insurance industry uses the term more broadly to include related forms of coverage, such as disability income insurance and long-term care insurance. Disability income (DI) insurance provides benefits to individuals who lose their ability to work due to injury or illness. Unlike medical expense insurance, which covers the cost of medical care, DI insurance replaces income lost during a period of disability. For most working-age adults, the risk of disability is greater than the risk of premature death, and the resulting reduction in lifetime earnings can be substantial. Private DI insurance is available on both a group and individual basis, with policies designed to cover either long-term disabilities (LTD coverage) or short-term disabilities (STD coverage). Business owners can also purchase disability overhead insurance to cover their business expenses while they are unable to work. A basic level of disability income protection is provided through the Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI) program for qualified workers who are totally and permanently disabled, meaning they are unable to engage in any substantial gainful work and their disability is expected to last at least 12 months or result in death. Long-term care (LTC) insurance reimburses policyholders for the cost of long-term or custodial care services, which are designed to minimize or compensate for the loss of functioning due to age, disability, or chronic illness. While LTC insurance shares some surface similarities with long-term disability insurance, there are fundamental differences. LTC policies cover the cost of certain types of chronic care, whereas long-term disability policies replace income lost while the policyholder is unable to work. For LTC insurance, the event triggering benefits is the need for chronic care, while for disability insurance, it is the inability to work. Private LTC insurance is becoming increasingly popular in the United States, with premiums remaining relatively stable in recent years.
